title: Generative AI and the Future of Artisan Teaching
author: Becky Allen
summary: Adapted from a researchED London talk, Becky Allen examines why the vast majority of English teachers still write their own lesson plans and resources rather than using pre-made materials, and asks what generative AI might do to that norm. She develops two analogies -- teachers as coders who resist inheriting someone else's codebase, and teachers as indie musicians who prefer writing their own material over performing others' compositions -- to explain the sense-making, ownership, and professional-identity motivations behind 'artisan teaching'. She also identifies structural, not just psychological, drivers: a UK 'textbook deficit' caused by underinvestment since the shift to interactive whiteboards, a deregulated curriculum that increases variability in what pre-made resources would need to cover, and the fact that lesson planning happens largely unpaid, shifting costs from schools onto individual teachers. She notes a striking contradiction in survey data -- two-thirds of teachers can't imagine using pre-prepared plans without adaptation, yet only a quarter say they most admire colleagues specifically for their resources -- and closes by describing generative AI as already used by a third of teachers for planning, positioning it as a tool that could support rather than replace the artisan model in the near term.
points: Allen's coder and indie-musician analogies both isolate the same underlying driver of artisan teaching: the sense-making and identity value of creating something from scratch, distinct from whether the created thing is actually higher quality.

Her structural explanation -- a 'textbook deficit' from underinvestment, a deregulated curriculum, and unpaid planning time shifting costs onto teachers -- reframes artisan teaching as partly a systemic default, not purely a matter of professional pride.

The survey contradiction she flags (two-thirds resist unadapted pre-made plans, yet only a quarter cite colleagues' resources as most admirable) is sharp evidence that teachers' stated attachment to self-made materials may outstrip their actual confidence in those materials' quality.

Her invocation of the Dunning-Kruger effect regarding teachers' confidence in their own lesson planning -- despite little formal training in curriculum theory or assessment design -- directly questions whether the artisan norm is actually producing better outcomes.
Framing AI as already used by a third of teachers for planning, rather than a future hypothetical, grounds the piece's forward-looking questions in a documented present-tense adoption rate.
quotes: Artisan teaching—where teachers create their own lesson plans and resources—remains a cornerstone of English schools.
Just as coders often insist on rewriting existing code from scratch, teachers frequently reject pre-prepared lesson plans and materials in favour of creating their own.
In the UK, however, teachers resemble indie musicians. They embrace the challenges of crafting bespoke lesson plans, relishing the dual pleasures of creation and delivery.
A significant challenge in the UK is the "textbook deficit." With the rise of technology like interactive whiteboards and online projection, schools have deprioritised purchasing textbooks.

While two-thirds of UK teachers say they cannot imagine regularly using pre-prepared lesson plans without adaptation, when asked about colleagues they most admired, only a quarter mention they admire the resources and plans they create.
Research suggests that the Dunning-Kruger effect—where individuals overestimate their expertise—may apply to curriculum planning.
Generative AI, such as ChatGPT, is already being used by a third of teachers, primarily for lesson planning.
